items.stem: Which term describes taking part in religious activities such as attendance, prayer and membership?
items.answer: Religious participation
items.markingKey: Religious participation: taking part in religious activities such as attendance, prayer and membership. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “feminisation of the church”, and give one example.
items.answer: The growing proportion of women among religious participants and clergy. Example: more women than men in church congregations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the growing proportion of women among religious participants and clergy); 1 mark for a relevant example such as more women than men in church congregations. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “structural location” and “feminisation of the church”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Structural location: the idea that women’s position in society (e.g. less paid work, more caring) increases their religiosity (e.g. more time for church activities). Feminisation of the church: the growing proportion of women among religious participants and clergy (e.g. more women than men in church congregations).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: In a congregation in Lagos, two-thirds of regular attenders are women, but all the senior leaders are men. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: religion has become a matter of individual choice and consumption; people pick and mix beliefs in a spiritual supermarket (Lyon, Heelas).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A survey in Istanbul finds that women in full-time work attend religious services less often than women who are not in paid work. Explain how a liberal feminist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Liberal feminism: gender differences in religiosity result from socialisation and women’s roles; as roles become more equal, differences narrow (Miller and Hoffmann).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of self-completion questionnaires for studying gender differences in religious attendance over time.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; they can reach a large, geographically spread sample quickly and cheaply, so findings can be generalised. Limitations: closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity; response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying gender differences in religious attendance over time but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes taking part in religious activities such as attendance, prayer and membership?
items.answer: Religious participation
items.markingKey: Religious participation: taking part in religious activities such as attendance, prayer and membership. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “gendered religiosity”?
items.answer: Differences between men and women in religious belief and practice.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: differences between men and women in religious belief and practice. [1]

items.stem: What is the difference between “gendered religiosity” and “socialisation explanation”?
items.answer: Gendered religiosity: differences between men and women in religious belief and practice. Socialisation explanation: the view that women are more religious because they are socialised to be caring, obedient and nurturing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “gendered religiosity” and “socialisation explanation”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Gendered religiosity: differences between men and women in religious belief and practice (e.g. women praying more often than men). Socialisation explanation: the view that women are more religious because they are socialised to be caring, obedient and nurturing (e.g. girls taught to be submissive and caring).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Priya, a sociology student, is designing a project on why women and men attend religious services. Explain one strength of using non-participant observation for this research.
items.answer: It records behaviour as it happens rather than relying on people’s accounts.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of why women and men attend religious services. [2]

items.stem: A survey in Cape Town finds that women in full-time work attend religious services less often than women who are not in paid work. Compare how liberal feminist and postmodernist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Liberal feminism: gender differences in religiosity result from socialisation and women’s roles; as roles become more equal, differences narrow (Miller and Hoffmann). Postmodernism: religion has become a matter of individual choice and consumption; people pick and mix beliefs in a spiritual supermarket (Lyon, Heelas).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: A survey of 300 adults in Mumbai produced the results below. Table: adults (%) | Women | Men. Pray at least weekly | 52% | 38%. Attend services at least monthly | 35% | 23%. Take part in New Age or holistic activities | 14% | 6%. (a) Calculate the difference between Take part in New Age or holistic activities and Attend services at least monthly for Women and for Men, and state for which of these the difference is larger. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that women are more religious than men.
items.answer: (a) Women: 21 percentage points; Men: 17 percentage points; the difference is larger for Women. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure is lower for Men than for Women among Pray at least weekly, Attend services at least monthly, Take part in New Age or holistic activities; Pray at least weekly had the highest figure for Men. New Age emphasis on healing appeals to women. Qualifications: Self-report may differ by gender; differences vary by age and religion; men may participate in other forms; one city may be untypical. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 300 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each difference (21 and 17); 1 mark for the correct comparison. [3] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “cultural transition”, and give one example.
items.answer: The use of religion to help migrants adjust to a new society. Example: churches supporting new arrivals.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the use of religion to help migrants adjust to a new society); 1 mark for a relevant example such as churches supporting new arrivals. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “diaspora religion” and “resurgence of religion”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Diaspora religion: religion practised by communities living outside their homeland (e.g. Hindu temples in cities across the world). Resurgence of religion: a revival in religious commitment, often among minority groups (e.g. second-generation migrants becoming more observant).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A temple in Seoul runs language classes, helps new migrants find work and holds festivals that bring the community together. Suggest how an interactionist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Interactionism: religion is a source of identity negotiated in interaction, especially in response to labelling and exclusion (Modood).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Isla, born in Singapore to migrant parents, has become more religious than her parents; she says that facing racism made her proud of her faith. Explain how a functionalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: religion integrates minority communities and helps migrants through cultural transition (Herberg).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of structured interviews for studying religious attendance among different ethnic groups.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; the interviewer can explain unclear questions, so fewer answers are spoiled. Limitations: the interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour; the interviewer’s presence may produce interviewer bias or socially desirable answers. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying religious attendance among different ethnic groups but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Explain Pryce’s argument that religion can help minority groups cope with racism and deprivation, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Pryce found Pentecostalism helped African-Caribbean people in Bristol adapt and gave them hope. Criticism: Rastafarianism offered resistance rather than adaptation.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Functionalism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.answer: 1. They are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid. 2. The interviewer’s presence may produce interviewer bias or socially desirable answers.

items.stem: A survey of 1200 minority ethnic adults in Kuala Lumpur compared migrants with their children born in the country. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that religion is declining among the second generation.
items.answer: (a) 64 − 74 = -10 percentage points (Second generation compared with First generation). (b) Evidence from the data: The figure is higher for Second generation than for First generation among Describe religion as central to their identity; the figure is lower for Second generation than for First generation among Say religion is “very important” to them, Attend a place of worship weekly; Describe religion as central to their identity had the highest figure for Second generation. items.stem: In a wealthy district of Mumbai, the established church is full every Sunday, while in a poor district nearby, small Pentecostal churches meet in rented halls. Explain how postmodernist and functionalist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Postmodernism: religion has become a matter of individual choice and consumption; people pick and mix beliefs in a spiritual supermarket (Lyon, Heelas). Functionalism: religion promotes social solidarity and value consensus, helps people cope with life crises and reinforces the collective conscience (Durkheim, Malinowski, Parsons).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of covert participant observation for studying why women and men attend religious services.
items.answer: Strengths: it can give access to closed or deviant groups who would refuse an overt researcher; it produces rich, first-hand qualitative data with high validity. Limitations: the researcher may be drawn into illegal or harmful activity and is at risk if discovered; the study cannot be repeated, so reliability is low. Theory: covert participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying why women and men attend religious services but best combined with another method such as official statistics (triangulation).

items.stem: A survey of 800 adults in Cairo produced the results below. Table: adults (%) | Women | Men. Pray at least weekly | 53% | 39%. Attend services at least monthly | 35% | 29%. Take part in New Age or holistic activities | 10% | 3%. (a) Using the data, identify the group with the highest figure for Men. (b) Calculate the difference between Pray at least weekly and Attend services at least monthly for Women and for Men, and state for which of these the difference is larger.
items.answer: (a) Pray at least weekly (39%). (b) Women: 18 percentage points; Men: 10 percentage points; the difference is larger for Women.
items.markingKey: (a) Pray at least weekly, 39%. [1] (b) 1 mark each difference (18 and 10); 1 mark for the correct comparison. [3]

items.stem: A survey in Cairo finds that women in full-time work attend religious services less often than women who are not in paid work. Explain how a postmodernist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Postmodernism: religion has become a matter of individual choice and consumption; people pick and mix beliefs in a spiritual supermarket (Lyon, Heelas).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A research team is investigating gender differences in religious attendance over time. Evaluate the use of self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; closed, pre-coded questions produce quantitative data that is easy to compare and turn into statistics. Limitations: response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative; closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying gender differences in religious attendance over time but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: A survey of 450 adults in Accra produced the results below. Table: adults (%) | Women | Men. Pray at least weekly | 51% | 36%. Attend services at least monthly | 28% | 20%. Take part in New Age or holistic activities | 12% | 4%. (a) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Women and Men for Pray at least weekly. (b) Explain one limitation of using self-completion questionnaires to collect data like these. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that women are more religious than men.
items.answer: (a) 36 − 51 = -15 percentage points (Men compared with Women). (b) Response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure is lower for Men than for Women among Pray at least weekly, Attend services at least monthly, Take part in New Age or holistic activities; Pray at least weekly had the highest figure for Men. New Age emphasis on healing appeals to women. Qualifications: Self-report may differ by gender; differences vary by age and religion; men may participate in other forms; one city may be untypical. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 450 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 51 and 36; 1 mark for 15 percentage points with direction. [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes a sense of self based on membership of a religious group?
items.answer: Religious identity
items.markingKey: Religious identity: a sense of self based on membership of a religious group. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “cultural transition”.
items.answer: The use of religion to help migrants adjust to a new society.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the use of religion to help migrants adjust to a new society. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Some second-generation migrants become more religious. Reason (R): religious organisations provide community, support and practical help (cultural transition). Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
items.answer: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
items.markingKey: A and R are both true statements, but R does not explain A. [1]

items.stem: Hana, born in Lima to migrant parents, has become more religious than her parents; she says that facing racism made her proud of her faith. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: young people combine religious and other identities, choosing how far religion matters to them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Sipho surveyed 500 minority ethnic adults in Mexico City. Table: minority ethnic adults (%) | First generation | Second generation. Say religion is “very important” to them | 69% | 60%. Attend a place of worship weekly | 49% | 36%. Describe religion as central to their identity | 63% | 53%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between First generation and Second generation for Say religion is “very important” to them (Second generation minus First generation)?
items.answer: -9 percentage points
items.markingKey: 60 − 69 = -9 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Ana surveyed 500 minority ethnic adults in Toronto. Table: minority ethnic adults (%) | First generation | Second generation. Say religion is “very important” to them | 78% | 63%. Attend a place of worship weekly | 51% | 32%. Describe religion as central to their identity | 66% | 71%. (a) Using the data, identify the group with the highest figure for Second generation. (b) Calculate the difference between Attend a place of worship weekly and Describe religion as central to their identity for First generation and for Second generation, and state for which of these the difference is larger. (c) Describe two patterns shown in the data.
items.answer: (a) Describe religion as central to their identity (71%). (b) First generation: 15 percentage points; Second generation: 39 percentage points; the difference is larger for Second generation. (c) The figure is higher for Second generation than for First generation among Describe religion as central to their identity; the figure is lower for Second generation than for First generation among Say religion is “very important” to them, Attend a place of worship weekly; Describe religion as central to their identity had the highest figure for Second generation.
items.markingKey: (a) Describe religion as central to their identity, 71%. [1] (b) 1 mark each difference (15 and 39); 1 mark for the correct comparison. [3] (c) 1 mark for each accurate pattern supported by figures from the table. [2]

items.stem: To what extent do sociological arguments and evidence support the view that religion is more important to minority ethnic groups than to the majority population?
items.answer: For: Modood; Bruce’s cultural defence and transition; Herberg; Pryce; religion and identity among second generation. Against: Religiosity declines over generations; variation between groups; some white groups are also religious; postmodern choice; secularisation affects all groups. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on how far the view holds.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): a few simple points. Level 2 (4-6): some explained arguments, mainly on one side; limited evaluation. Level 3 (7-9): a range of explained arguments and evidence for and against, with some evaluation. Level 4 (10-12): a balanced, well-supported analysis using theories, studies and concepts, sustained evaluation and a reasoned conclusion. For: Modood; Bruce’s cultural defence and transition; Herberg; Pryce; religion and identity among second generation. Against: Religiosity declines over generations; variation between groups; some white groups are also religious; postmodern choice; secularisation affects all groups. [12]

items.stem: Which term describes a religious justification of the privileges of the wealthy?
items.answer: Theodicy of good fortune
items.markingKey: Theodicy of good fortune: a religious justification of the privileges of the wealthy. [1]

items.stem: Briefly explain Weber’s view that different classes are attracted to different religious ideas and organisations.
items.answer: Weber argued the poor are drawn to a theodicy of disprivilege and the wealthy to religions that justify their position.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the idea; 1 mark for developing it: Weber argued the poor are drawn to a theodicy of disprivilege and the wealthy to religions that justify their position. [2]

items.stem: Glock and Stark argued that different types of deprivation lead people to different religious organisations. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: They identified economic, social, organismic, ethical and psychic deprivation. Criticism: Deprivation is hard to measure and many deprived people are not religious.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Weberian theory); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: A survey of 240 adults in Doha produced the results below. Table: adults (%) | Middle class | Working class. Attend an established church | 24% | 12%. Attend a sect or Pentecostal church | 6% | 10%. Take part in New Age activities | 6% | 4%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Middle class and Working class for Attend a sect or Pentecostal church (Working class minus Middle class)?
items.answer: +4 percentage points
items.markingKey: 10 − 6 = +4 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: A research team is investigating why people in poorer areas join small churches. Evaluate the use of self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they can reach a large, geographically spread sample quickly and cheaply, so findings can be generalised; closed, pre-coded questions produce quantitative data that is easy to compare and turn into statistics. Limitations: pre-set answers cannot capture the subjective meanings people attach to their experiences; respondents may misunderstand questions, or give socially desirable answers, and there is no chance to clarify. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying why people in poorer areas join small churches but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]
